title: Your First Drive
outcome: Make the basic decisions that appear on almost every drive.

lessons.title: The Light Changes. What Now?
lessons.objective: Traffic lights look simple. The situation around them may not be.

intro.summary: Traffic lights look simple. The situation around them may not be.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: Your light is green, but traffic blocks the other side.

blocks.title: Green means check first
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A green light lets you move only when the intersection is clear.

Check the intersection before you go.

“Green means go” is incomplete.

Yield to pedestrians and traffic that still has priority.

Protected and permitted movements are not the same.

blocks.title: Let people clear the road
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Someone may still be in the intersection.

Let pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles clear your path.

Green allows movement, but it does not make a blocked or unsafe path legal.

Yield to pedestrians and vehicles still in the intersection.

Do not enter if traffic will leave you stopped in the intersection.

Check again before turning, especially for bicycles and pedestrians.

blocks.title: Yellow means decide safely
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Yellow means the light is changing.

Stop if you can do it safely.

A circular green signal permits the applicable movement, but the intersection must be usable and any required yield still applies.

A steady yellow warns that the green movement is ending and red will follow.

Do not race the change; stop when you can do so safely.

blocks.title: Red means stop
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Make a complete stop.

Use the limit line.

If there is no line, stop before the crosswalk.

A right turn on red has extra conditions.

In California, this turn is usually allowed after a full stop.

A sign may prohibit it.

Yield before you turn.

At a steady circular red, stop at the limit line, before the near crosswalk, or before entering the intersection when neither exists.

A permitted turn after stopping still requires a clear path, the proper yield, and no sign prohibiting that turn.

A red arrow prohibits its indicated movement until a signal permits it.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Right on red is usually allowed after a full [[stop]] — unless a [[sign]] prohibits it.

blocks.title: Arrows control one direction
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
An arrow controls the direction it points.

A red arrow means stop and wait.

Pedestrian indications control when people may start crossing, but drivers must still protect pedestrians lawfully in or entering the roadway.

Countdown or flashing-hand phases do not give turning drivers permission to crowd someone who has not finished crossing.

blocks.title: Flashing signals
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Flashing red works like a STOP sign.

Flashing yellow means slow down and use caution.

Flashing red means stop at the lawful point, then proceed under stop-sign rules when safe.

Flashing yellow means proceed with caution; A flashing yellow does not require an automatic stop.

Overhead lane-control signals also differ: green permits lane use, red closes it, and yellow warns of a change.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Flashing [[red]] works like a STOP sign. Flashing [[yellow]] means slow down and use caution.

blocks.title: A dark signal
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Treat a broken signal like an all-way stop.

Move carefully.

Other drivers may read the dark signal differently, so expect hesitation.

A signal that has lost power needs a cautious, predictable response.

Slow down and prepare to stop.

Treat the intersection like an all-way stop unless a sign or officer directs otherwise.

Take turns and do not assume another driver has noticed the outage.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: A dark signal? Treat the intersection as an [[all-way stop]].

blocks.title: Remember the full picture
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
The light is only the first clue.

Check arrows, signs, people, traffic, and space ahead.

Signal colors do not answer every question by themselves.

First identify the indication, then the movement it controls, and finally the traffic or pedestrians you must still yield to.

This three-step habit prevents most signal-question traps.

lessons.title: STOP, YIELD, or Keep Going?
lessons.objective: Three simple controls can create very different decisions.

intro.summary: Three simple controls can create very different decisions.
keyPoints: Enter only when you can clear.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: A YIELD sign faces you. Cross traffic is close.

blocks.title: STOP means zero movement
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Slow down early.

Stop fully before moving again.

After the complete stop, scan for vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians.

If a building or parked vehicle blocks the view, move forward only as needed and only after protecting the crosswalk.

A gap that existed when the wheels stopped can close before you move.

blocks.title: Use the first stopping point
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
When there is a limit line, stop before your vehicle reaches it.

If there is no line, use the crosswalk or intersection edge.

At a stop sign, stop at the marked limit line.

If there is no line, stop before the near-side crosswalk.

If neither exists, stop at the nearest point where you can see approaching traffic before entering the intersection.

Keep the vehicle out of pedestrian space.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Stop before the [[limit line]]. If there is no line, use the [[crosswalk]] or the intersection edge.

blocks.title: A blocked view changes the next step
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Make the required stop first.

Then creep forward slowly for a better view.

A blocked view does not erase the first required stop.

Stop at the limit line, crosswalk, or intersection edge as the situation requires.

After stopping and yielding, edge forward slowly for a better view.

Stop again if a new conflict appears.

blocks.title: YIELD is not a rolling STOP
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Slow enough to judge the gap.

Stop only when traffic or people require it.

At a yield sign, slow to a reasonable speed, stop if necessary, and yield to traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard.

If the path is clearly open, an automatic stop is not required.

If a safe gap does not exist, continue yielding.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: YIELD means slow down, judge the [[gap]], and [[stop]] when traffic requires it.

blocks.title: Driveways join active traffic
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
People already on the road go first.

Check sidewalks, bikes, and both traffic directions.

One exam answer may stop in the right place but fail to yield before entering.

Another may yield but block the crosswalk.

Both answers ignore part of the required stop-and-yield sequence.

A complete solution must protect the stopping point and the moving path.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Entering the road from a [[driveway]] or private property? Yield until it is [[safe]].

blocks.title: Do not enter a trap
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Wait when you cannot clear the intersection.

The same idea applies at railroad tracks.

A green light or your turn at a stop does not allow you to block the conflict area.

Wait before an intersection when traffic is backed up beyond it.

Wait before tracks until your entire vehicle can fit on the far side.

Keep crosswalks clear for pedestrians and mobility-device users.

blocks.title: Never force your priority
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A correct rule cannot prevent another driver’s mistake.

Yield again if a crash is developing.

A driver leaving a driveway, alley, or private property must yield to nearby traffic.

Keep yielding until it is safe to enter.

Cross the sidewalk only after checking for pedestrians, wheelchairs, bicycles, and other users who may be hidden by walls or landscaping.

blocks.title: Remember this order
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
STOP, YIELD, and driveway questions use the same basic pattern.

Control the car before the conflict.

Then yield until it is safe to move.

The stopping point and the later visibility check are separate steps.

At a STOP or YIELD conflict, keep this order:

lessons.title: Make a Safe Turn
lessons.objective: A safe turn starts before the steering wheel moves.

intro.summary: A safe turn starts before the steering wheel moves.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: You plan to turn right across a bicycle lane.

blocks.title: A turn has four parts
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Break every turn into the same short sequence.

Choose the legal lane before the turn.

Signal and reduce speed while checking all sides.

Yield to pedestrians, bicycles, and opposing traffic.

Complete the turn into a legal lane without drifting.

Use the same four-part sequence for every turn:

blocks.title: Signal before the turn
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Give other people time to react.

In California, signal during the final 100 feet.

For a lane change or other lateral movement, signal when another vehicle may be affected and move only when reasonably safe.

A signal communicates intent; it does not order another road user to make space.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: In California, signal continuously during the final [[100 feet]] before your turn.

blocks.title: Right turns start near the right edge
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Move into the legal turn position.

Watch for cyclists between you and the curb.

Right and left turns must begin and end from the positions required for the roadway.

Do not swing wide from the wrong lane or cut across multiple lanes on exit.

Marked arrows, bicycle-lane conditions, and multiple-turn lanes can change the allowed path, so read them early.

blocks.title: Left turns cross more traffic
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Yield to approaching traffic.

Turn only when the gap is safe.

A driver turning left or making a U-turn must yield to approaching traffic close enough to be hazardous.

After yielding, complete the turn only when reasonably safe.

A green circular signal may permit the turn, but it does not automatically protect it from oncoming traffic.

blocks.title: Do not cut the corner
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Stay on your side while entering the intersection.

Finish in a lane that permits your movement.

Good turns are prepared before the steering begins.

The driver communicates, chooses the lawful starting position, clears pedestrians and traffic, and follows a predictable path into the correct lane.

blocks.title: One-way streets change the setup
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Signs and arrows show the legal turn lane.

Check the destination street before you move.

A transit-only or bicycle lane is not a general travel lane, but a posted or statutory exception may allow entry for a turn.

Check signs and markings before entering.

Enter only where and when permitted for the maneuver.

Yield to users already traveling in that lane.

blocks.title: Cancel the signal
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A forgotten signal tells a false story.

Make sure it turns off after the maneuver.

The signal is not the maneuver.

An answer can mention signaling and still be wrong if the lane, blind-spot check, yield, or receiving path is unsafe.

blocks.title: Turn checklist
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Use your left arm for hand signals.

Hold it straight out for a left turn.

Point it up for a right turn.

Point it down to slow or stop.

California law gives bicyclists another option.

Before turning across a bicycle lane, check your mirrors and blind spot.

Yield to any bicyclist already in that space.

Run through this checklist before and during the turn:

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Left arm straight out: [[left]] turn. Arm up: [[right]] turn. Arm down: [[slow]] or stop.

lessons.title: Keep Space Around Your Car
lessons.objective: Speed and distance buy you time when something changes.

intro.summary: Speed and distance buy you time when something changes.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: The limit is 55 mph. Heavy fog hides the road ahead.

blocks.title: The limit is not a target
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A posted limit assumes good conditions.

Rain, fog, traffic, or glare may require less.

The safe speed can be lower than the sign when conditions reduce your margin.

Slow for rain, fog, darkness, curves, hills, traffic, and road work.

Choose a speed that lets you stop within the distance you can see.

Never drive faster than is safe for current conditions.

blocks.title: California uses the Basic Speed Law
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Never drive faster than conditions allow.

You can be too fast below the posted limit.

Consider weather, visibility, traffic, the road surface, and road width.

Never use a speed that puts people or property in danger.

A posted maximum is not a command to maintain that speed.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Never drive faster than is [[safe]] for current conditions, even below the posted [[limit]].

blocks.title: Look beyond the next car
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Scan far enough to see trouble early.

Early changes are smoother and safer.

Keep your eyes moving ahead, to the sides, behind, and through intersections.

A hazard seen early usually needs a small response.

The same hazard discovered at the bumper needs a hard response and may leave no safe path.

blocks.title: Leave a time gap
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Pick a fixed point ahead.

Count after the vehicle in front passes it.

Add more time when risk grows.

California prohibits following more closely than is reasonable and prudent for the leading vehicle's speed, the traffic, and roadway conditions.

A time-gap technique can help estimate space, but poor weather, darkness, a motorcycle, or a large vehicle may require more.

blocks.title: Stopping takes three stages
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
The car travels while you perceive the hazard, while you decide and react, and while the brakes reduce speed.

Higher speed and poor traction enlarge the total space.

Looking farther ahead does not shorten braking physics, but it lets you begin sooner.

Total stopping distance has three stages:
bullets: Only then do the brakes slow the car.

blocks.title: Keep an escape space
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Avoid sitting beside another vehicle.

Leave room to move if traffic stops suddenly.

Avoid driving boxed in beside other vehicles.

Leave room around parked cars, merging traffic, bicycles, and uncertain drivers.

If a conflict develops ahead, a usable side space may prevent a rear-end collision when braking alone is not enough.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Leave a [[time]] gap to the car ahead and keep an [[escape space]] beside you.

blocks.title: Handle a tailgater calmly
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Create more room ahead.

Change lanes or use a turnout when safe.

Do not brake-check.

Trying to teach a close follower a lesson increases the danger.

Increase the space ahead so you can slow gradually.

Avoid sudden braking, speeding up, or blocking a pass.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: You stop in three stages: you [[see]] the problem, you [[react]], and only then the brakes slow the car.

blocks.title: Remember the goal
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
See early.

Leave space.

Slow before the situation becomes urgent.

Open space gives you time to notice a problem and respond smoothly.

The goal is not to protect one memorized number; it is to keep enough room to notice, decide, brake, or steer without transferring the emergency to another road user.

title: Read the Road
outcome: Read signs, warnings, lines, arrows, and curb controls quickly.

lessons.title: Sign Shapes Give You a Head Start
lessons.objective: A sign can warn you before every word becomes readable.

intro.summary: A sign can warn you before every word becomes readable.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: You see a red eight-sided sign ahead.

blocks.title: Start with the family
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Shape and color give you an early clue.

They help before the details are clear.

Regulatory signs tell road users what is required or prohibited.

Warning signs call attention to a condition that may demand an early adjustment.

Guide signs help with routes, destinations, and services.

This first classification narrows the meaning before you read the details.

blocks.title: The octagon means STOP
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Eight sides have one traffic meaning.

Prepare for a complete stop.

Traffic signs are designed to work at a glance.

You do not need to memorize every sign as an isolated picture.

First identify its family, then read the symbol or words, and finally connect it to the decision you must make.

blocks.title: The downward triangle means YIELD
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Slow down and scan for conflicts.

Stop if someone needs the space.

Some shapes are deliberately unique.

An octagon identifies STOP.

A downward-pointing triangle identifies YIELD.

A pennant warns of a no-passing zone, and a pentagon marks a school-related area.

Recognizing these silhouettes buys time when visibility is poor or the sign is partly blocked.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: The eight-sided octagon always means [[STOP]]. The downward triangle always means [[YIELD]].

blocks.title: The round sign warns about tracks
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A railroad crossing is ahead.

Look for gates, lights, and a clear exit.

A sign is easier to read when you do not treat it as one big picture.

First: identify the family from shape and color.

Second: read the symbol, words, arrow, or plaque.

Third: turn the message into an action you can take now.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: A [[round]] sign warns that [[railroad]] tracks are ahead.

blocks.title: The pentagon marks a school area
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Expect children near the road.

Slow down and scan the sidewalks.

Do not treat color as the complete answer.

Two signs may share a color but require very different actions.

On an exam, identify the family quickly, then use the symbol, wording, placement, and any plaque to choose the exact response.

blocks.title: A diamond warns
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
The symbol shows the type of hazard you are approaching.

Change your speed or position early, while you still have room.

Shape and color help you predict the message, but the sign's words, symbol, plaque, lane position, and operating times determine the real instruction.

A sign mounted over one lane may apply only to that lane.

A time plaque can make a restriction active only during stated hours.

blocks.title: Colors support the message
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Red is strongly associated with stopping or prohibition.

Yellow calls attention to general warnings.

Orange is used for temporary traffic-control and work activity.

Green, blue, and brown commonly guide rather than command.

Color is a clue—not permission to ignore the actual symbol, words, or roadway context.

Use these color families as quick clues:

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: [[Red]] restricts. [[Yellow]] warns. [[Orange]] means work zones.

blocks.title: The exact message wins
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Shape and color help you identify the sign before you read every detail.

Words, symbols, arrows, and plaques give the full rule.

Shape and color help you predict a sign, but they do not replace its actual instruction.

A plaque may limit a rule to certain hours or vehicles.

An overhead sign may control only the lane below it.

Road conditions and an officer’s directions can change what you do next.

lessons.title: Signs That Tell You What to Do
lessons.objective: Regulatory signs control a specific action, lane, vehicle, or time.

intro.summary: Regulatory signs control a specific action, lane, vehicle, or time.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: A police officer waves you through a red light.

blocks.title: Read the sign as a verb
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Ask which action the sign controls.

The fastest exam strategy is to ask what action the sign controls.

STOP means make a complete stop at the lawful stopping point.

YIELD means give way and stop if needed.

Turn, entry, speed, lane-use, and parking signs control a specific choice.

Start by naming the action:

blocks.title: White rectangles give exact rules
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
They often control speed, turns, parking, or lane use.

Read the full message.

STOP requires a complete stop at the lawful stopping point before you evaluate the path.

YIELD requires you to slow enough to give way and stop when necessary.

In both cases, proceed only after the conflicting path is clear; the difference is whether a stop is always required.

blocks.title: A red slash means no
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
The symbol shows the prohibited move.

Do not perform that action.

A regulatory sign does not grant right-of-way simply because you obeyed it.

After stopping or following a lane instruction, you still must yield to traffic or pedestrians lawfully in the conflict area.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: A red circle with a slash means that movement is [[not allowed]].

blocks.title: DO NOT ENTER protects one direction
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
The road or ramp is closed to your movement.

Choose another legal path.

You must obey a traffic sign or signal that applies to you unless an authorized officer directs otherwise or a legal exception applies.

Follow an officer who directs you through a red light.

Keep watching for people and drivers who may not expect the temporary traffic pattern.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: DO NOT ENTER protects [[one direction]] of traffic — WRONG WAY means you are already against it.

blocks.title: WRONG WAY means act now
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Slow down.

Move out of opposing traffic without creating another hazard.

DO NOT ENTER protects the entrance; WRONG WAY warns that you are facing traffic moving toward you.

Do not continue deeper into the roadway.

Slow, stop in the safest available position, and reverse direction only when you can do so without creating another conflict.

blocks.title: Plaques narrow the rule
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A rule may apply only at certain times.

It may target one lane or vehicle type.

Turn-prohibition, one-way, lane-use, speed, entry, and parking signs regulate a particular choice.

Read the arrow, vehicle symbol, lane placement, and plaque.

A NO LEFT TURN sign does not automatically prohibit going straight, and an HOV sign does not automatically apply outside its posted conditions.

blocks.title: People can direct traffic
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
An authorized officer or flagger may override the normal pattern.

Move carefully.

Traffic may be directed differently during an emergency, collision, or special operation.

Follow a peace officer or other person legally authorized to direct traffic.

Keep watching for pedestrians and drivers who may not understand the temporary pattern.

Do not assume obeying a signal gives you the right-of-way over someone already in danger.

blocks.title: Exam shortcut
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Find the controlled action first.

Then check lane, time, vehicle, and exception.

Regulatory signs turn road design into clear instructions.

The useful exam skill is not simply naming the sign.

It is identifying the controlled movement, lane, vehicle, time, or place and acting before you enter the restricted area.

lessons.title: Signs That Warn You Early
lessons.objective: A warning sign gives you time. Use that time before the hazard.

intro.summary: A warning sign gives you time. Use that time before the hazard.
keyPoints: Use guide signs without sudden moves.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: A LANE ENDS sign appears ahead.

blocks.title: Warnings buy you time
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Look farther ahead.

Prepare before the road changes.

A warning sign does not tell you one fixed speed or maneuver.

The warning gives you time to prepare before the road changes.

Adjust speed and lane position before the hazard.

Expect the risk to be hidden around a curve, hill, work area, or crossing.

blocks.title: The symbol names the problem
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Curves, merges, crossings, and slippery roads use clear symbols.

Match your action to the hazard.

Do not start across tracks unless there is enough room for your whole vehicle on the far side.

Stop when required by a signal, gate, flagger, or approaching rail vehicle.

Never drive around, under, or through a closed or moving gate.

Treat stopped traffic beyond the tracks as a reason to wait before the crossing.

blocks.title: Advisory speed is about the hazard
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
It suggests a safer speed for the condition ahead.

It is not the general speed limit.

Curve, crossroad, merging, divided-highway, lane-ending, slippery-surface, and signal-ahead signs preview the road or traffic pattern.

Identify the hazard, check the surrounding traffic, and make the smallest early speed or lane adjustment that preserves control.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: A yellow advisory speed describes the [[hazard]] — it is not a separate legal limit.

blocks.title: School signs widen your scan
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Watch sidewalks, parked cars, and crosswalks.

A child may appear from the side.

A school-area pentagon or pedestrian warning shifts your attention beyond vehicle traffic.

Look toward sidewalks, parked cars, crossing points, and people who may enter the roadway.

The sign warns of the environment; any posted speed or crossing control supplies the exact legal instruction.

blocks.title: Railroad warnings need an exit plan
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Never enter tracks without room beyond them.

A train cannot steer around you.

Railroad advance signs tell you to look, listen, and prepare for crossing controls.

Never begin across tracks unless space on the far side can hold the entire vehicle.

A train cannot steer away, and entering behind another vehicle can trap you even when the warning equipment was clear at first.

blocks.title: Orange means temporary work
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Slow down.

Expect workers, equipment, closed lanes, and flaggers.

Work-zone signs, cones, drums, barriers, arrow boards, and flaggers can replace the normal path.

Reduce speed for the actual conditions, increase space, and follow the temporary channel.

Green, blue, and brown guide signs usually support navigation; read them early so you do not cut across traffic.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: [[Orange]] warning signs mean a [[temporary]] work zone ahead.

blocks.title: Guide signs help you plan
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Warning and special-area signs are advance information.

They let you trade a sudden reaction for an early, controlled adjustment.

Guide signs serve a different purpose: they help you choose a route or service without creating a last-second lane change.

The color gives you a quick clue:

blocks.title: Missed the sign?
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Continue safely.

Do not make a sudden turn or reverse to recover the route.

A warning sign does not automatically set right-of-way or a universal speed.

It tells you what to expect.

Apply any posted regulation and then choose a speed that is safe for the actual sight distance, surface, traffic, and people present.

lessons.title: Lines, Arrows, and Curb Colors
lessons.objective: The road surface tells you where to drive, stop, and turn.

intro.summary: The road surface tells you where to drive, stop, and turn.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: A stop sign has a painted limit line.

blocks.title: Color tells you the traffic relationship
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Yellow lines usually separate traffic moving in opposite directions.

White usually separates traffic moving together.

Yellow markings normally separate traffic moving in opposite directions or mark specified left-edge conditions.

White markings normally separate lanes moving in the same direction and mark the right edge.

Start with color before interpreting broken, solid, or double patterns.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: [[Yellow]] lines separate opposite directions. [[White]] lines separate lanes going the same way.

blocks.title: Pattern tells you about crossing
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Broken lines may allow crossing when safe.

Solid lines warn or restrict it.

A broken line generally marks a place where crossing may be allowed when the maneuver is otherwise legal and safe.

A solid line warns or restricts crossing.

Double solid white lines form a lane barrier; wait for a permitted opening or broken pattern instead of forcing a lane change.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: A [[broken]] line allows crossing when safe. A [[solid]] line restricts it.

blocks.title: Double lines need attention
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Do not treat every double line the same.

Color, spacing, and road context matter.

Do not answer a marking question from color alone.

Yellow versus white identifies the traffic relationship; broken, solid, double, arrows, signs, and roadway context determine the permitted movement.

blocks.title: Arrows assign a movement
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Choose the lane before the last moment.

Follow the arrow painted in your lane.

Road markings are a language under your tires.

Color identifies the relationship between traffic streams; pattern shows whether crossing is permitted or restricted; arrows and painted areas organize where movements belong.

blocks.title: Limit lines show where to stop
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Stop before the line.

Keep crosswalks clear.

Limit lines and crosswalk markings show where the front of your vehicle should stop.

Stop before the limit line when one is present.

If there is no limit line, stop before the crosswalk.

Move forward only as needed for visibility after the required stop and after yielding.

blocks.title: Painted islands are not travel lanes
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Stay out unless markings allow entry.

Do not use them to pass a queue.

A single set of double solid yellow lines generally bars passing across the center, while limited turns may be allowed where another rule permits.

Two sets of double lines spaced two feet or more apart form a barrier.

Do not drive on or across it.

Use only a marked opening or another legally allowed path.

blocks.title: Curb colors control stopping
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Red, white, green, yellow, and blue have different uses.

Check signs for details.

Each curb color has a different job:
bullets: A red curb means no stopping, standing, or parking, except at a marked bus zone.
A yellow curb is for loading or unloading within the local time limit.
A white curb is for passengers or a marked mail area.
A green curb allows parking for a limited time.
A blue curb is only for authorized disabled parking.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: A [[red]] curb means no stopping, standing, or parking. A [[blue]] curb is only for authorized disabled parking.

blocks.title: Read markings in layers
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
One marking rarely tells the whole story.

Color tells you whether traffic usually moves in the same or opposite directions.

Broken or solid patterns show where crossing is permitted or restricted.

Arrows and words assign movements to particular lanes.

Read the road surface in this order:
bullets: Then arrows, signs, and nearby traffic.

title: Intersections and Everyday Moves
outcome: Handle right-of-way, people, backing, U-turns, and parking.

lessons.title: Who Goes First?
lessons.objective: Right-of-way rules organize movement. They do not remove danger.

intro.summary: Right-of-way rules organize movement. They do not remove danger.
keyPoints: Look right when arrival is tied.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: Two cars reach an uncontrolled intersection together.

blocks.title: Someone already inside goes first
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Let the intersection clear.

Do not challenge a vehicle already in your path.

If another vehicle is already inside the intersection, let it clear before you enter.

Do not use your speed or arrival story to challenge someone who is physically in the conflict area.

Slow early and keep an escape option.

blocks.title: Arrival order organizes the queue
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
The first clear arrival normally moves first.

A driver who arrives later should wait for the earlier vehicle.

When one road user clearly arrives first, that person normally proceeds first after checking the intersection.

The useful clue is not which vehicle is larger or moving faster; it is the order in which each reaches the decision point.

blocks.title: Same time? Look right
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
The driver on the left yields.

Confirm that the other driver is actually moving.

If two vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection together, the vehicle on the right goes first.

The same left-yields-right pattern applies when the intersection is controlled from all directions by stop signs after both vehicles stop.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Arriving together? The [[left]] driver yields to the driver on the [[right]].

blocks.title: A T-intersection has a continuing road
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Traffic on the ending road yields.

People in the intersection still come first.

At an uncontrolled T-intersection, traffic on the continuing road goes first.

This is not permission for through traffic to ignore a collision risk—both drivers still watch, slow, and protect people in the intersection.

blocks.title: Blocked views demand less speed
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Cover the brake.

Move only far enough to see.

The goal is to prevent two road users from choosing the same space.

Slow enough to see cross traffic, bicycles, and pedestrians.

Yield when the rule requires it or when proceeding would cause a crash.

Do not insist on priority when another person is already moving into the conflict.

blocks.title: Eye contact is not a legal signal
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A driver may look at you and still move.

Trust space and speed, not a glance.

Right-of-way rules make crossing paths predictable.

They do not create a shield around the vehicle that technically goes first.

Use the rule to organize movement, then confirm that the other road user is actually yielding before entering the conflict.

blocks.title: Mountain roads have a special rule
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
When neither car can pass, the downhill-facing driver normally backs up.

Use the nearest safe space.

When two vehicles meet on a steep, narrow road and neither can pass, the vehicle facing downhill is generally better able to back up.

The descending vehicle must yield and back up when necessary.

Use the nearest safe place rather than squeezing past.

Drive at a speed that lets you stop within the road you can see.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: On a narrow mountain road, the vehicle facing [[downhill]] backs up to make room.

blocks.title: Right-of-way is never forced
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Give up your turn when a crash is developing.

Safety beats being technically first.

Right-of-way is something the other road user yields; it is not something you force.

If another driver fails to follow the sequence, give up the turn rather than turn a correct exam answer into a crash.

lessons.title: People in Your Path
lessons.objective: Pedestrians can be hard to see and have no protection from your car.

intro.summary: Pedestrians can be hard to see and have no protection from your car.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: A car is stopped at a crosswalk in the next lane.

blocks.title: A crosswalk may be unmarked
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Intersection corners can form a crosswalk without painted lines.

Scan both sides.

A pedestrian crossing outside a marked or unmarked crosswalk must yield to vehicles close enough to be an immediate hazard.

Drivers still owe due care and must avoid injury when possible.

A blind pedestrian using a predominantly white cane or guide dog receives specific protection; yield and take necessary precautions.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: A crosswalk can be [[unmarked]] — pedestrian right-of-way still applies.

blocks.title: Slow before the person appears
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Parked cars and large vehicles can block your view.

Expect movement from the side.

A pedestrian may be difficult to see until you are very close.

Scan sidewalks, corners, parked vehicles, and median islands.

Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk.

Wait until the pedestrian is safely out of your path before proceeding.

blocks.title: Do not pass a stopped crosswalk vehicle
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
It may be protecting someone you cannot see.

Stop and check.

Do not overtake and pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross.

The stopped vehicle blocks your view and may be the only clue that someone is in front of it.

Cover the brake and wait until the entire crossing is visible and safe.

blocks.title: Blind pedestrians need predictable traffic
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A white cane or guide dog is an important clue.

Stop and stay quiet.

A white cane or guide dog tells you that a pedestrian may rely on traffic sounds and predictable vehicle movement.

Stop and yield; do not use the horn to invite the person across.

Do not block the crosswalk or stop so close that engine noise is misleading.

Remain still until the person is safely clear of your path.

blocks.title: Do not wave someone into danger
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Another lane may still be moving.

Yield without giving a risky signal.

Yield to a pedestrian crossing within a marked or unmarked crosswalk and exercise due care.

A pedestrian must not suddenly enter so close that a driver cannot stop safely, but that condition does not remove the driver's duty to watch, slow, and avoid a collision.

blocks.title: Roundabout traffic already inside goes first
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Slow before the entry.

Choose a safe gap and enter in the correct direction.

Approaches to a roundabout are controlled so entering traffic yields to traffic already circulating.

Slow, read the signs and lane arrows, choose the lane before entry, and enter only into a usable gap.

Follow the indicated one-way circulation and signal lane changes or the exit when required.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Never pass a vehicle [[stopped]] at a crosswalk. Entering a roundabout, yield to traffic [[already inside]].

blocks.title: Choose the roundabout lane early
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Signs and arrows show the lane for your exit.

Avoid changing lanes inside.

“The pedestrian should have yielded” is not a safe answer if the driver can still prevent harm.

The test may ask who had a duty and what the driver should do next; those are related but not identical questions.

blocks.title: Exit with a final check
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Signal when useful.

Watch the crosswalk beyond the roundabout.

Pedestrian safety questions are about what you cannot see as much as what you can.

Crosswalk rules, blind-pedestrian protections, and roundabout entry controls all reward the same habit: approach slowly enough to discover the conflict before entering it.

lessons.title: Driveways, Backing, and U-Turns
lessons.objective: Slow maneuvers still create serious conflicts.

intro.summary: Slow maneuvers still create serious conflicts.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: You miss your freeway exit.

blocks.title: Check before the car moves
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Walk around when a child or object may be hidden.

Use mirrors and a shoulder check.

Mirrors and cameras help, but they do not show every person or object.

Walk around the vehicle first when the area may hide a child or obstacle.

Look over the appropriate shoulder and back at walking speed.

Stop whenever your view becomes uncertain.

blocks.title: Back slowly
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Look in the direction you are moving.

Stop when the view becomes uncertain.

Do not start from a stopped, standing, or parked position or back on a highway until the movement can be made with reasonable safety.

Check behind, beside, and for small road users hidden below the windows.

Move slowly enough to stop immediately if the scene changes.

blocks.title: Cameras do not show everything
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A lens can miss low, close, or side hazards.

Use it as one tool, not the only tool.

At a signal-controlled intersection, a U-turn must be permitted by the applicable signal rule and begin from the far-left lawful lane.

In a business district, a U-turn is prohibited except at an intersection or a provided opening on a divided highway.

blocks.title: Driveways cross sidewalks
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Yield to people before entering the road.

Then find a safe traffic gap.

In a residence district, do not make a U-turn when another vehicle is approaching from either direction within 200 feet.

An exception applies at an intersection where a traffic-control device controls the approaching vehicle.

Estimate conservatively; the purpose is a clear, usable gap.

blocks.title: A U-turn needs legal space
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Check signs, lane position, traffic, and visibility.

Possible does not always mean legal.

A U-turn can look physically possible and still be illegal because of the location, visibility, or approaching traffic.

Backing has the same underlying rule: begin only when the movement can be made with reasonable safety.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: A U-turn needs an unobstructed view for [[200 feet]] in both directions.

blocks.title: California uses a 200-foot visibility test
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
You need a clear view in both directions.

Other location rules can still prohibit the turn.

A U-turn is prohibited unless the driver has an unobstructed view for 200 feet in both directions.

Do not make one in front of a fire station or use its driveway approaches to reverse direction.

Meeting the visibility test does not cancel the location prohibition.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: No U-turns in front of a [[fire station]] — ever.

blocks.title: Fire stations and business districts add limits
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Read the exact location in the question.

Do not apply one U-turn rule everywhere.

Do not reduce U-turn questions to a single 200-foot number.

The exam may change the location, signal control, visibility, business or residential context, or fire-station fact.

blocks.title: Missed your move?
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Continue to a legal place.

A wrong route is safer than a sudden reversal.

A missed turn or driveway is not an emergency.

Continue to a place where you can turn around legally.

Do not back on a freeway or across traffic to recover a missed exit.

Make a U-turn only when it is legal and you can see far enough in both directions.

lessons.title: Park Without Getting a Ticket
lessons.objective: Good parking protects visibility, access, and moving traffic.

intro.summary: Good parking protects visibility, access, and moving traffic.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: You park downhill beside a curb.
blocks.questionPreview: Where should the front wheels point?

blocks.title: Check the place before the technique
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A perfect parking move is still illegal in a prohibited spot.

Read signs and curb color first.

Stay at least 15 feet from a fire hydrant unless a legal exception applies.

Red curb means no stopping, standing, or parking; green is time-limited; white and yellow serve defined loading purposes; blue is restricted to authorized disabled parking.

Posted local time limits still control how long you may park.

blocks.title: Parallel parking stays slow
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Signal and check around the car.

Back in gradually and center the vehicle.

Accuracy comes from low speed and repeated checks, not one fast steering move.

Signal and stop beside the vehicle ahead of the space.

Check mirrors, blind spots, pedestrians, bicycles, and traffic.

Back slowly into the space, straighten, and center without touching other vehicles.

blocks.title: Stay close to the curb
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
California generally requires parking within 18 inches.

One-way roads can change the allowed side.

On a roadway, park in the lawful direction and generally within 18 inches of the appropriate curb, subject to one-way and local provisions.

Before leaving, stop the engine and set the parking brake.

On a hill, turn the front wheels so a rolling car moves away from danger.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Park within [[18 inches]] of the curb and at least [[15 feet]] from a fire hydrant.

blocks.title: Secure the car
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Set the parking brake.

Use Park or the correct gear before leaving.

Section 22500 lists places where stopping, standing, or parking is prohibited, subject to traffic, safety, officer-direction, and other exceptions.

Common conflicts include sidewalks, crosswalks, driveways, and locations where the vehicle blocks traffic or access.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Turn the wheels so a rolling car goes toward the [[curb]] or edge, and set the [[parking brake]].

blocks.title: Hill parking controls a possible roll
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
With a curb, turn the wheels so the curb can stop the car.

Without a curb, turn toward the road edge.

Wheel direction is only one part of hill parking.

Set the parking brake and place the transmission in Park or the proper gear.

Turn the wheels so a rolling vehicle moves toward the curb or edge rather than traffic.

Before pulling out, signal and check traffic and blind spots.

blocks.title: Hydrants need clear space
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
In California, keep at least 15 feet of space from a fire hydrant.

A legal exception must be clear.

“I will be quick” does not erase a prohibited stopping place.

The law may regulate stopping or standing even when the driver stays in the car.

blocks.title: Blue spaces are protected
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Use them only with valid authorization.

Keep access aisles clear.

Parking rules protect sight lines, access, traffic flow, and people who must cross or open doors.

Solve them by checking the place, measured clearance, curb control, vehicle position, and safe exit.

blocks.title: Leaving is another maneuver
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Signal.

Check mirrors and blind spots.

Enter only when the gap is safe.

Open a door into moving traffic only when reasonably safe and leave it open no longer than necessary.

Check for bicycles and motorcycles before exiting.

On a fully controlled-access freeway, stopping is exceptional; a real emergency should be handled as far from moving lanes as possible.

title: Lanes, Passing, and Freeways
outcome: Choose lanes, pass safely, merge, and use special lanes.

lessons.title: Choose the Right Lane
lessons.objective: Good lane choices prevent sudden moves later.

intro.summary: Good lane choices prevent sudden moves later.
keyPoints: Change one lane at a time.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: Your mirror looks clear before a lane change.

blocks.title: Choose early
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Use signs, arrows, and your route.

Last-second lane changes create extra risk.

On a two-lane highway, a slow vehicle may have to use a turnout when passing is unsafe.

The rule applies when five or more vehicles are following.

Use a marked turnout or another safe area.

Do not pull off where the surface or sight distance makes the cure more dangerous than the delay.

blocks.title: Use the full check
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A turn signal shows what you plan to do.

It does not give you the right to move.

Check mirrors for traffic approaching from behind.

Look over your shoulder for the blind spot.

Move only when the gap is large enough.

Do not force another driver to brake.

Check the space in this order:

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Before moving sideways: signal, mirrors, then a head check of the [[blind spot]].

blocks.title: One lane at a time
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Finish one lane change before starting another.

Keep the signal useful and clear.

Drive on the right half of the road unless an exception applies.

Examples include legal passing, avoiding an obstruction, or driving on a one-way road.

When moving slower than traffic, stay in the right lane or near the right edge.

Move left when passing or preparing for a left turn.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Change [[one]] lane at a time — settle, recheck, then move again.

blocks.title: Do not camp beside another car
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
That car may need your lane.

Move ahead or drop back when safe.

Keep the vehicle as nearly as practical within a single lane.

Do not drift across a line while searching for a gap.

Before moving, check traffic ahead, beside, and behind; signal when others may be affected; and wait until the destination lane has enough usable space.

blocks.title: Traffic breaks need patience
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
An officer may weave to slow traffic.

Do not pass or race the controlled pattern.

Law enforcement may slow or weave across lanes to create space ahead for a hazard or operation.

Do not try to pass the patrol vehicle.

Reduce speed smoothly and follow its directions.

Expect stopped traffic or an incident beyond the point you can see.

blocks.title: A lane can end quickly
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Plan a merge when the warning appears.

Do not wait for the pavement to disappear.

A mirror shows only the angle reflected into it.

Motorcycles, bicycles, and cars can travel in the uncovered zone slightly behind either side.

Turn your head enough to check through the side window without turning the steering wheel or your whole body.

blocks.title: Missed the lane?
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Continue safely and reroute.

Do not cut across traffic or painted barriers.

A signal is a request for space, not proof that space exists.

An answer that says “signal and move” but omits observation can still be wrong.

Make your move predictable.

Signal early enough to help.

Use a steady speed and smooth path.

Lane discipline makes your vehicle predictable.

Choose a lane that fits your speed and next move.

Stay centered.

Before moving sideways, signal and check the space yourself.

lessons.title: Pass—or Wait?
lessons.objective: Passing needs legal permission, enough sight distance, and a safe return.

intro.summary: Passing needs legal permission, enough sight distance, and a safe return.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: A hill hides the road ahead on a two-lane road.

blocks.title: Passing begins with permission
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Check signs and lane markings.

A safe-looking gap does not cancel a restriction.

Curves, grades, intersections, and railroad approaches can create legal no-passing conditions when visibility and distance rules apply.

A quick maneuver does not remove the hidden conflict.

Read signs and markings, but also identify the roadway feature.

blocks.title: See the complete path
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
You need room to move out, pass, and return.

Do not guess beyond a hill or curve.

Do not move into oncoming traffic until you can see far enough ahead.

Make sure the lane stays clear for the entire pass.

If you cannot see the full decision, you do not have a passing opportunity.

blocks.title: Check behind before moving out
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Another driver may already be passing.

Use mirrors and a blind-spot check.

Overtake safely to the left unless a specific right-side rule applies.

Do not return to the original lane until you are safely clear of the vehicle.

Check mirrors and blind spots before both the outward move and the return.

blocks.title: Pass with a clear speed difference
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Do not stay beside the other vehicle.

Finish without exceeding the legal speed.

A pass must be both legal and safe for the conditions.

A legal location can still be unsafe because of sight distance, oncoming traffic, speed difference, a bicycle, or the space needed to return.

blocks.title: Return with space
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
See the passed vehicle clearly in your mirror.

Do not cut closely in front.

Do not begin with only enough space to pull out.

See the full distance needed to pass and return.

Check for driveways, intersections, hills, curves, and changing markings.

Cancel the pass early if any part of the plan becomes uncertain.

blocks.title: Never pass near certain conflicts
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Crossings, intersections, bridges, and blocked views may prohibit passing.

Read the exact scenario.

Right-side passing is allowed only in listed roadway situations and only when it can be completed safely.

Never leave the paved or main-traveled portion to get around another vehicle.

A shoulder is not a bonus passing lane.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Do not move into oncoming traffic until you can see far enough [[ahead]] to complete the whole pass.

blocks.title: When someone passes you
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Keep a steady path.

Do not speed up.

Create room if needed.

The shoulder and unpaved area are not ordinary passing lanes.

Do not leave the paved or main-traveled part of the roadway to pass.

When being passed, hold a steady course and do not increase speed.

Make room when safe instead of competing with the passing driver.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Skip the pass near an intersection, a railroad [[crossing]], or a hidden [[curve]].

blocks.title: Waiting is a valid decision
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A few seconds can remove the risk.

Pass only when every part of the path works.

“The line is broken” answers only one part of the question.

Look for a hidden curve, hill, intersection, railroad crossing, oncoming vehicle, or insufficient return gap.

lessons.title: Enter and Leave the Freeway
lessons.objective: Freeway driving works best when speed and lane choices are planned early.

intro.summary: Freeway driving works best when speed and lane choices are planned early.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: You are entering from an acceleration lane.

blocks.title: Use the ramp to prepare
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Build speed while scanning traffic.

Do not wait until the merge point to look.

Begin scanning the freeway while you still have ramp length.

Identify the speed and spacing of several vehicles, not just one.

A gap is useful only if you can reach it without an abrupt acceleration, brake, or sideways cut.

blocks.title: Freeway traffic has priority
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Find a gap and adjust smoothly.

Do not force another driver to brake.

Use the acceleration lane to approach the freeway's flow while staying within the applicable law and conditions.

A large speed difference makes the merge harder for everyone.

Do not assume freeway traffic must yield; enter only when the lane movement is reasonably safe.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Freeway traffic has [[priority]]. Use the whole [[acceleration lane]] to match its speed.

blocks.title: Use the whole acceleration lane
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
More lane gives you more time.

Stop only when traffic leaves no safe alternative.

The acceleration lane gives you time to observe traffic and adjust speed.

Find a gap before you reach the merge point.

Match the flow without exceeding a safe and legal speed.

Yield to freeway traffic already in the lane.

blocks.title: Once inside, rebuild space
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Check your following gap.

Avoid staying beside another vehicle.

Stopping, standing, or parking on a fully controlled-access freeway is prohibited except for specific safety, legal, work, disability, or designated-location situations.

If a real emergency forces a stop, move as far from traffic as possible and make the vehicle visible.

blocks.title: Plan the exit early
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Read signs and move into the correct lane.

Signal before the exit.

Read guide signs early.

Move toward the exit one safe lane at a time.

Slow in the exit lane when appropriate.

If you miss the exit, continue to the next safe route; do not reverse, stop, or cross a painted gore.

blocks.title: Slow on the exit ramp
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Leave freeway traffic at a stable speed.

Reduce speed where the ramp allows it.

Freeway questions reward early observation.

Use the ramp and auxiliary lane to understand the traffic stream, choose a gap, and make one smooth merge.

Last-second moves create larger speed differences and smaller options.

blocks.title: Missed the exit?
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Take the next one.

Never stop, back up, or cross a gore area.

Yielding on a ramp does not mean an automatic stop.

Stopping can erase the speed and distance needed to merge.

Choose the action that fits the traffic, sign, and available lane—not a universal ramp ritual.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Missed the exit? Continue to the [[next]] one — never stop or [[back up]] on the freeway.

blocks.title: Ramp signals control entry
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Stop when the meter is red.

Enter on the permitted signal and merge normally.

A metering signal spaces vehicles entering a freeway.

Stop at red at the marked line.

Proceed on green for the number of vehicles shown by the sign.

After the signal, use the rest of the ramp to merge normally.

lessons.title: Lanes with Special Rules
lessons.objective: Some lanes are legal only for a certain move, vehicle, or time.

intro.summary: Some lanes are legal only for a certain move, vehicle, or time.
keyPoints: Watch for people already in the lane.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: You want to enter an HOV lane.

blocks.title: A special lane has a specific job
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Identify the lane before entering.

Do not treat it as ordinary travel space.

Special lanes are defined by the combination of markings, signs, users, and operating times.

Treating them like ordinary travel lanes is a common exam error.

blocks.title: Center-turn lanes are for turns
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Use them to prepare for a legal left turn or U-turn.

Do not cruise or pass in them.

The number 200 appears in several California rules.

The exam may swap center-turn-lane distance with U-turn visibility or bicycle-lane turn entry.

Read what the distance is measuring.

blocks.title: California limits center-lane travel
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Do not travel more than 200 feet in the lane.

Watch for opposing drivers using it too.

Enter the shared center lane only to prepare for and make a lawful left turn or U-turn.

Look for opposing drivers who may enter the same lane for their own turns.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: In a two-way left-turn lane, travel no more than [[200 feet]].

blocks.title: Bicycle lanes carry real traffic
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Check behind before crossing one.

Enter for a turn only where allowed.

A motor vehicle may enter a bicycle lane only for the permitted parking, roadway-entry, or turning purposes.

For turn preparation, the law uses a 200-foot limit.

Before crossing or entering, check the blind spot and yield to a bicyclist already using the lane.

blocks.title: HOV and toll lanes use posted rules
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Check occupancy, vehicle type, time, toll, and access point.

Do not assume.

Use a preferential lane only when your occupancy, vehicle class, access point, and time meet the signs and markings.

Do not assume yesterday's hours or another freeway's occupancy rule applies here.

Enter and leave only at permitted openings.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: HOV and toll lanes work only under their [[posted]] rules — occupancy, hours, and permits.

blocks.title: Transit lanes are not shortcuts
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A limited entry may be allowed for a turn.

Yield to buses or other authorized users.

A special lane’s rules may change by location, time, direction, or vehicle.

Read occupancy, vehicle, time, and toll conditions before entering.

Follow solid and broken access markings.

Do not assume a rule from one freeway applies to another.

blocks.title: Barriers are not passing areas
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Two separated sets of double lines form a barrier.

Do not drive across it.

Two sets of double parallel lines spaced two feet or more apart form a barrier.

A two-way left-turn lane has a different marking pattern and exists for permitted left turns or U-turns.

Do not use either space as an ordinary passing lane.

blocks.title: Use turnouts when required and safe
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A slow vehicle may need to let traffic pass.

Reenter only with a safe gap.

Transit lanes reserve space for specified vehicles; turnouts let a slower vehicle release a queue.

Do not use a transit-only lane as a general travel lane.

Use a turnout when required and safe to let following traffic pass.

title: Share the Road
outcome: Protect road users who move, stop, and see differently.

lessons.title: Bicycles and Motorcycles
lessons.objective: Smaller road users are easy to hide and easy to injure.

intro.summary: Smaller road users are easy to hide and easy to injure.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: You plan to open a door beside moving traffic.

blocks.title: Look where riders can disappear
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Check mirrors and blind spots.

Look again before turning or changing lanes.

Before entering or crossing a bicycle lane, check mirrors and the blind spot for a rider beside or behind you.

Merge behind the bicyclist when necessary rather than turning across the rider's path.

A signal does not make the bicycle disappear.

blocks.title: Bicycle lanes carry traffic
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A cyclist may approach from behind.

Yield before crossing the lane.

Bicycles and motorcycles are narrow, easy to hide, and entitled to road space.

The safest driver detects them before turning or changing lanes and avoids making their small size an excuse for a small margin.

blocks.title: Expect movement away from the edge
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Debris, drains, and parked doors can push a cyclist left.

Leave room.

A bicyclist may be beside you even when the travel lane looked clear a moment ago.

Check the bicycle lane and right-side blind spot before turning.

Look behind before opening a door next to traffic.

Expect a bicyclist to leave the edge to avoid debris, drains, or parked cars.

blocks.title: Pass with space
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
California requires at least three feet when possible.

Change lanes when needed and safe.

When passing a bicycle, keep at least three feet.

When practicable and lawful, change lanes to pass a bicyclist in the same lane.

If neither option can be completed without danger, slow and remain behind until the situation improves.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Give a bicycle at least [[three feet]] of clearance when passing — slow down if you cannot.

blocks.title: A motorcycle owns its lane
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Do not squeeze beside it.

Use a normal lane-change gap.

Motorcycles can disappear in blind spots and can look farther away or slower than they are.

Look again before changing lanes.

Leave a safe following gap.

Never squeeze past a motorcycle while both vehicles are in one lane.

Road defects may require a rider to shift position quickly.

blocks.title: Their speed is hard to judge
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
A narrow profile looks farther away.

Check twice before turning across its path.

Their narrow profile makes speed and distance harder to judge.

Give a full lane and normal following space.

Check twice before turning or changing lanes.

Do not share a lane with a motorcycle or block lawful lane splitting.

blocks.title: Lane splitting is legal in California
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Do not block or crowd a rider doing it lawfully.

Stay predictable.

California law defines lane splitting as a two-wheeled motorcycle traveling between rows of stopped or moving vehicles.

A car driver should not block, chase, or deliberately narrow the available space.

Check before opening a door or moving laterally, even in slow traffic.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: A motorcycle is entitled to its [[full lane]]. Lane splitting is [[legal]] in California.

blocks.title: The safety rule is simple
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Search longer.

Leave more room.

Never assume the rider saw you.

A bicycle or motorcycle is not required to vanish because your turn or pass would be convenient.

Questions often test whether you wait for a safe gap instead of compressing a vulnerable road user.

lessons.title: Trucks, Buses, and Slow Vehicles
lessons.objective: Large vehicles need more room. Slow vehicles change closing speed.

intro.summary: Large vehicles need more room. Slow vehicles change closing speed.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: A truck starts a wide right turn.

blocks.title: Large vehicles have large blind spots
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
If you cannot see the driver in a mirror, the driver may not see you.

Move out of the no-zone.

A large vehicle can have extensive blind areas immediately in front, behind, and along both sides.

Avoid lingering and do not cut closely in front after passing.

blocks.title: They need more stopping room
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Do not cut closely in front.

Leave extra space after passing.

A truck driver may be unable to see a car close to the front, rear, or sides.

If you cannot see the driver in a mirror, assume the driver may not see you.

Leave extra room on grades and at stops because a heavy vehicle needs more space.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: If you cannot see the truck driver in a [[mirror]], the driver may not see [[you]].

blocks.title: Wide turns use two paths
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
The cab may first swing away from the direction of the turn.

The rear wheels may track close to the curb.

Trucks and buses may swing outward before turning or track rear wheels closer to the curb than the cab.

Never enter the space between a turning large vehicle and the curb.

Wait until the complete vehicle clears the path.

Never squeeze beside a turning truck.

The open space can disappear.

Wait behind the vehicle.

The open space beside a large vehicle may be space the vehicle is about to use.

Road geometry—not impatience—predicts the conflict.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Never cut [[closely]] in front of a truck — it needs far more [[stopping room]].

blocks.title: Pass without lingering
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Move through the blind spot steadily.

Return only when the truck is clearly visible in your mirror.

Buses, streetcars, and light rail follow routes that can place passengers or rails beside ordinary traffic.

Follow signs, signals, lane markings, and boarding-island rules.

Do not turn across the path of an approaching rail vehicle.

Watch for passengers crossing between a curb and a transit stop.

blocks.title: Slow vehicles change your timing
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
You may close the gap faster than expected.

Brake early and wait for a legal pass.

Large vehicles follow the same road rules but need different geometry: wider turns, larger blind areas, and more stopping space.

Slow vehicles and animals add another lesson—predict movement before you arrive beside it.

blocks.title: Animals can react suddenly
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Slow down near riders or livestock.

Follow the rider’s signal when an animal is frightened.

A slower driver on a two-lane road may need a turnout when five or more vehicles queue under the legal conditions.

Near horses or livestock, reduce speed or stop as needed and follow the handler's directions.

Avoid horns, revving, or abrupt movement that can frighten an animal.

blocks.title: Give size the space it needs
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
More room helps everyone see, stop, and turn.

A heavy vehicle may need more room to slow and may gain speed downhill.

After passing, remain ahead long enough to create a usable gap before returning.

When following, leave space so you can see around the vehicle and react without relying on its driver.

lessons.title: School Buses and Emergency Vehicles
lessons.objective: Some vehicles and people need the road cleared immediately.

intro.summary: Some vehicles and people need the road cleared immediately.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: An ambulance approaches from behind with lights and siren.

blocks.title: Emergency vehicles need a clear path
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Check around you.

Move toward the right edge and stop when safe.

When an emergency vehicle approaches with lights or a siren, move toward the right edge.

Stop away from intersections and wait until it passes.

Follow any officer's directions.

A divided highway may have a different rule.

If already in an intersection, clear it before pulling over.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Emergency vehicle with lights or siren? Pull to the [[right]] edge and [[stop]] clear of intersections.

blocks.title: Do not stop in the conflict
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Clear the intersection first when necessary.

Then stop where responders can pass.

Look for more responders.

One vehicle may be followed by several more.

Check before reentering traffic.

An emergency vehicle needs a predictable path.

Check around you before moving toward the required side and stopping.

Do not stop in an intersection or block the emergency route.

After it passes, check for additional responders before reentering traffic.

blocks.title: Protect vehicles stopped on the roadside
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Move over when the law requires and space allows.

Otherwise slow down safely.

Since 2026, California extends this protection to any stopped vehicle displaying warning or hazard lights, not only emergency vehicles.

Approaching a qualifying stationary vehicle displaying emergency, amber, hazard, or other warning devices, move to a nonadjacent available lane when practicable and lawful.

If you cannot, slow to a reasonable and prudent safe speed.

The rule does not apply when a barrier separates the vehicle or it is not adjacent to the highway.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Passing a stopped vehicle with warning lights: move to a [[nonadjacent]] lane, or [[slow]] to a safe speed.

blocks.title: Do not follow the response
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
California prohibits following a responding emergency vehicle within 300 feet.

Give the scene room.

Stay at least 300 feet behind a responding emergency vehicle unless authorized.

Never drive over an unprotected fire hose unless the fire department commander allows it.

Extra space keeps the route and scene available to responders.

blocks.title: School-bus red lights mean stop
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Stop while the red signals flash.

Watch for children crossing.

Stop when a school bus flashes red lights or extends its stop arm.

Stay stopped until the warning ends.

Different rules may apply on divided or multilane highways.

A divided road can change who stops.

Read the median and road design carefully.

Do not invent an exception on an ordinary road.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Flashing [[red]] school-bus lights mean stop — and stay stopped until the signal [[ends]].

blocks.title: People can control traffic too
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Follow authorized crossing guards and officers.

Stay stopped until they release your movement.

A crossing guard, flagger, or authorized officer may direct traffic through a temporary pattern.

Obey the person’s signal even when it differs from the normal signal or lane.

Slow early and expect workers, children, equipment, or stopped traffic.

Do not resume normal speed until you are clear of the controlled area.

lessons.title: Railroads, Light Rail, and Work Zones
lessons.objective: Tracks and temporary lanes punish last-second decisions.

intro.summary: Tracks and temporary lanes punish last-second decisions.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: Traffic is stopped just beyond railroad tracks.

blocks.title: Tracks need an exit
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Check the space beyond the rails.

Wait before the crossing when traffic is backed up.

Do not start across tracks unless there is enough room for your whole vehicle on the far side.

Stop when required by a signal, gate, flagger, or approaching rail vehicle.

Never drive around, under, or through a closed or moving gate.

Treat stopped traffic beyond the tracks as a reason to wait before the crossing.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Cross the tracks only when you can see a clear [[exit]] on the other side.

blocks.title: A train cannot avoid you
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Never race it.

Stop for lights, gates, flaggers, and an approaching train.

Railroad advance signs tell you to look, listen, and prepare for crossing controls.

Never begin across tracks unless space on the far side can hold the entire vehicle.

A train cannot steer away, and entering behind another vehicle can trap you even when the warning equipment was clear at first.

Never go around a gate.

A second train may be hidden.

Wait until the control fully allows movement.

If the vehicle stalls on the tracks, get everyone out immediately.

Move everyone away from the rails.

Use the crossing emergency sign, then call 911.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Stalled on the tracks? Get everyone [[out]] and away immediately.

blocks.title: Light rail shares city space
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Check signals, signs, and the rail path.

Never turn in front of an approaching rail vehicle.

Buses, streetcars, and light rail follow routes that can place passengers or rails beside ordinary traffic.

Follow signs, signals, lane markings, and boarding-island rules.

Do not turn across the path of an approaching rail vehicle.

Watch for passengers crossing between a curb and a transit stop.

blocks.title: Orange means the road may change
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Expect narrow lanes, workers, equipment, and sudden queues.

Slow down early.

A crossing guard, flagger, or authorized officer may direct traffic through a temporary pattern.

Obey the person’s signal even when it differs from the normal signal or lane.

Slow early and expect workers, children, equipment, or stopped traffic.

Do not resume normal speed until you are clear of the controlled area.

blocks.title: Flaggers give real directions
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Follow the flagger even when the usual signal differs.

Do not move until released.

Stay stopped until the warning ends.

Different rules may apply on divided or multilane highways.

In work zones, follow temporary signs, channelizing devices, and flagger directions; expect narrowed lanes and sudden slowing.

blocks.title: Leave the work zone calmly
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Keep the lower safe speed until you are fully clear.

Watch for traffic merging back.

Work-zone signs, cones, drums, barriers, arrow boards, and flaggers can replace the normal path.

Reduce speed for the actual conditions, increase space, and follow the temporary channel.

title: When Driving Gets Hard
outcome: Stay in control when visibility, traction, or the vehicle fails.

lessons.title: Driving After Dark
lessons.objective: At night, you must control speed with the road you can actually see.

intro.summary: At night, you must control speed with the road you can actually see.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: Your headlights cannot show enough road for your current stopping distance.

blocks.title: Headlights help others see you
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
They do more than light the road.

Use them whenever visibility rules require.

Never drive faster than is reasonable for darkness, fog, smoke, rain, glare, or traffic.

Keep stopping distance within the visible usable path.

If you cannot see enough road to stop safely, reduce speed further or leave the roadway at a safe place.

blocks.title: Do not outrun your lights
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
You need enough visible road to stop.

Slow down before dark curves and hills.

If your stopping distance is longer than your visible road, a hidden hazard can become unavoidable.

Slow before dark curves, crests, fog banks, smoke, or heavy rain.

Use low beams in fog or smoke because high beams reflect light back.

Keep the windshield, lights, mirrors, and wipers clean and working.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Do not outrun your headlights — be able to [[stop]] inside the distance you can [[see]].

blocks.title: High beams have limits
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Dim within 500 feet of an approaching vehicle.

Dim within 300 feet when following.

Dim high beams for an approaching vehicle within 500 feet and when following another vehicle within 300 feet.

Looking toward the right edge can reduce glare from an oncoming driver, but you must still maintain lane position and a speed that fits what you can see.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Dim within [[500 feet]] of an approaching vehicle and within [[300 feet]] when following.

blocks.title: Glare steals detail
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Look toward the right road edge.

Reduce speed without staring at oncoming lights.

Sun glare, dust, snow, flooding, or strong wind can remove your normal safety margin.

Slow smoothly and increase following distance.

Use lane markings or the right road edge as a guide without staring at oncoming lights.

If you cannot see well enough to drive, leave the roadway at a safe place and wait.

blocks.title: Interior light can hurt night vision
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Keep the dashboard readable but not bright.

Put the phone away.

Clean glass matters.

Dust and streaks scatter light.

Keep windows, mirrors, and lamps clear.

Watch for what has no light.

Pedestrians, animals, debris, and parked cars may appear late.

Scan the edges.

blocks.title: Night rule
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
When you can see less, slow down.

Give yourself more time and more space.

Low visibility and poor traction shrink the time available to solve a problem.

The cure is not a brighter or faster response; it is a calmer one—see what you can, stay within that distance, and leave more room.

lessons.title: Rain, Fog, Heat, and Mountain Roads
lessons.objective: Bad conditions reduce the grip and visibility you normally trust.

intro.summary: Bad conditions reduce the grip and visibility you normally trust.

blocks.title: What would you do?
blocks.scenario: Heavy fog reflects your high beams back at you.

blocks.title: Rain changes two things
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Rain reduces visibility as well as tire grip.

Your tires also have less grip.

Rain, snow, wind, standing water, or loose surface calls for reduced speed, increased following space, and smooth steering, braking, and acceleration.

If hydroplaning begins, ease speed down progressively and avoid abrupt braking or steering that can turn reduced grip into a skid.

blocks.title: Can you finish the rule?
blocks.ruleMarkdown: Rain cuts [[grip]] and [[visibility]] — slow down and smooth every control.

blocks.title: Make every control smoother
blocks.bodyMarkdown:
Sun glare, dust, snow, flooding, or strong wind can remove your normal safety margin.
